You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test does:
  - testSevenEmptyFiles delegates to testCompress252(7, 0).
  - It builds an archive containing:
    - One directory entry "foo/" (via createArchiveEntry + putArchiveEntry + closeArchiveEntry with no data written).
    - Seven file entries "foo/0.txt" … "foo/6.txt", each written with an empty byte array and then closed.

- How entries are recorded:
  - putArchiveEntry simply enqueues the SevenZArchiveEntry into an internal list (files.add(entry)).
  - For empty writes, write(byte[], int, int) short-circuits when len == 0, so no output stream is created.
  - closeArchiveEntry detects no data written (fileBytesWritten == 0) and marks the entry as:
    - hasStream = false
    - size = 0
    - compressedSize = 0
    - hasCrc = false
  - This happens for all eight entries (the directory and the seven files).

- Where things go wrong:
  - 7z format represents per-entry booleans (hasStream, isDirectory, emptyFile, etc.) as bit-packed arrays in the header, with one bit per entry, packed into bytes (8 flags per byte).
  - In this scenario there are exactly 8 entries (1 dir + 7 files), i.e., exactly one full byte of flags.
  - The existing implementation’s header-writing logic for these boolean arrays (the bit-packing) is incorrect at the “multiple of 8” boundary. This is the classic COMPRESS-252 issue the test is named after.
    - The code writes the flags using an erroneous grouping (effectively treating the group size as 7 rather than 8, or mishandling the last/full byte), which corrupts the FilesInfo section when the number of entries reaches 8 (or more).
    - As a result, tools (and the test verifier) observe a malformed header: the archive is interpreted incorrectly (manifesting as a single folder entry named after the archive instead of the expected directory + seven empty files).

- Why it only shows with ≥ 8 entries:
  - With ≤ 7 entries, the single byte of flags isn’t filled, so the off-by-one/packing bug doesn’t get triggered.
  - With 8 entries (exactly one full byte), the faulty logic produces an incorrect flags byte (or mis-handles the boundary), which compromises the header parsing.

- Summary of root cause:
  - The method that serializes boolean vectors into the 7z header (bit-packing of per-entry flags) mishandles cases where the number of entries is a multiple of 8, causing incorrect FilesInfo metadata for archives containing only empty entries once they reach 8 total entries. This leads to corrupt or misinterpreted archives, matching the reported behavior and the failing test.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).

Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test does:
  - testSevenEmptyFiles delegates to testCompress252(7, 0).
  - It builds an archive containing:
    - One directory entry "foo/" (via createArchiveEntry + putArchiveEntry + closeArchiveEntry with no data written).
    - Seven file entries "foo/0.txt" … "foo/6.txt", each written with an empty byte array and then closed.

- How entries are recorded:
  - putArchiveEntry simply enqueues the SevenZArchiveEntry into an internal list (files.add(entry)).
  - For empty writes, write(byte[], int, int) short-circuits when len == 0, so no output stream is created.
  - closeArchiveEntry detects no data written (fileBytesWritten == 0) and marks the entry as:
    - hasStream = false
    - size = 0
    - compressedSize = 0
    - hasCrc = false
  - This happens for all eight entries (the directory and the seven files).

- Where things go wrong:
  - 7z format represents per-entry booleans (hasStream, isDirectory, emptyFile, etc.) as bit-packed arrays in the header, with one bit per entry, packed into bytes (8 flags per byte).
  - In this scenario there are exactly 8 entries (1 dir + 7 files), i.e., exactly one full byte of flags.
  - The existing implementation’s header-writing logic for these boolean arrays (the bit-packing) is incorrect at the “multiple of 8” boundary. This is the classic COMPRESS-252 issue the test is named after.
    - The code writes the flags using an erroneous grouping (effectively treating the group size as 7 rather than 8, or mishandling the last/full byte), which corrupts the FilesInfo section when the number of entries reaches 8 (or more).
    - As a result, tools (and the test verifier) observe a malformed header: the archive is interpreted incorrectly (manifesting as a single folder entry named after the archive instead of the expected directory + seven empty files).

- Why it only shows with ≥ 8 entries:
  - With ≤ 7 entries, the single byte of flags isn’t filled, so the off-by-one/packing bug doesn’t get triggered.
  - With 8 entries (exactly one full byte), the faulty logic produces an incorrect flags byte (or mis-handles the boundary), which compromises the header parsing.

- Summary of root cause:
  - The method that serializes boolean vectors into the 7z header (bit-packing of per-entry flags) mishandles cases where the number of entries is a multiple of 8, causing incorrect FilesInfo metadata for archives containing only empty entries once they reach 8 total entries. This leads to corrupt or misinterpreted archives, matching the reported behavior and the failing test.
